Cesta presentation interface, version 2

Every presentation interprets into the same C AST. A native view
checks each proposed abbreviation by expanding it and comparing the resulting
tree. Exact constructors remain available, and their children can be abbreviated.
Conversion expands the input presentation and views the result in the output
presentation. Source printing additionally checks source-grammar derivability.

ast/1 is the AST itself: explicit c: constructors and ordered c:List fields.
compact-c/2 is the current written form of C. Literals are the atoms their C
spellings read as: 42, 0x2au and 'a' are symbols and "hi\n" is a string, so
the token spelling is the atom's printed form; a spelling that is not exactly
one atom's printed form keeps its exact text in (char ...) or (strings ...).
Specifier sequences are flat C words, (static inline int); structures,
unions and enumerations are (struct node (int value)), (struct node) and
(enum color RED (= GREEN 4) BLUE); declarations are (var ...), (decl ...) and
(typedef T name); type names are (char *) or plain words; sizeof, typeof and
alignment of a type are written (sizeof type T). Calls splice their arguments,
(call f a b), and parameter lists may close with ... .
compact-c/1 is the first compact version, retained: literal atoms are
strings containing exact C token spellings, and its specifier, structure and
enumeration forms name grammar constructors.
cmera-style/1 adds independently written function and pointer spellings and
inherits the common compact-c/1 forms. Its *name spellings are opaque symbol
atoms for host pattern matching. It is a non-structural presentation, without
Common Lisp reader, macro-environment or full C-Mera compatibility claims.

Examples:
  (unit (fn void bump ((unsigned (* p))) (+= (* p) 1u)))
  (unit (fn void bump ((unsigned (* p))) (+= (* p) "1u")))      compact-c/1
  (unit (function bump ((unsigned *p)) -> void (+= *p "1u")))  cmera-style/1

Documents record the presentation/version, AST-schema identity and actual
rule-data identity. An unknown version or changed schema/rule identity is
refused. Raw .cesta authoring defaults to compact-c/2; sealed documents select
their declared presentation, so a sealed compact-c/1 document keeps reading
while the AST schema is unchanged.
Calls use an explicit call form, so adding an unrelated head does not
reinterpret a function call.

A schema step adds AST constructors, such as GNU label attributes
(label done ((__attribute__ unused)) (return 0)). It changes the schema
identity, so documents sealed before it are refused. Every presentation gains
a form for each new constructor and keeps every existing form: a retained
version still writes and reads every earlier tree the same way.

Rule forms

A surface rule describes atoms, not characters. A word is one symbol; a token
category alone is the token in its own representation (an identifier symbol,
or a string holding a literal's exact spelling); a prefix and a token category
are one symbol, and the empty prefix "" writes a token as the atom its
spelling reads as. A list form begins with a fixed word (a headed form) or
with a field (a tuple). Fixed words may appear among the fields, a list field
in last field position is spliced into the form, and fixed words may close the
spliced list, as in (function f (int a) ...). A "." before the last field
makes it a dotted tail: (static . rest) is written (static inline int) when
rest is the list (inline int), and (static size_t) when rest is one atom.
A rule with a token, word or list shape takes precedence over an unheaded rule
of its sort; several unheaded rules are allowed when their targets accept
disjoint atoms.

Dispatch is one-atom lookahead over S-expressions. Every sort has first-atom
keys: the symbols, strings and list heads its atoms can begin with, its exact
c: heads included. Two rules of a sort are refused when, at some common length,
every position can hold one atom under both; otherwise the rule whose shape
matches and whose positions admit the atom's items is selected. The keys
over-approximate the atoms that decode, so admission never refuses a valid
atom, and the view still keeps a short form only when it expands back to the
same tree. Sorts are the grammar's coercion classes, so rules for categories
joined by unit coercions, such as unique and primitive type specifiers,
dispatch together.

The portable/1 wire quotes symbol, text and expression kinds as ordinary MeTTa
data, using hexadecimal bytes. It supports ordinary CeTTa, PeTTa and HE readers
without relying on their registrations for names or numbers. Wire size is a
separate transport measurement from compact presentation payload size.

Shared module adapter

C AST theories and presentation theories are read through the same
grammar/TheoryModule.cf adapter and the same native module/catalog algebra.
Presentation Terms and Equations introduce ordinary declarations in this
adapter; they do not use another .module parser. The metta-venus grammar and
fixtures are historical compatibility inputs, not the specification of an
unchangeable final language.

Imports resolve named modules and instantiate their theory parameters. Exports
and replacements retain their declaration identities. The origin-coherent
composition profile requires one structural view per origin; origin-view
composition retains distinct structural declarations at a shared origin while
requiring exposed labels to identify declarations uniquely. The corresponding
Lean algebras distinguish these admission and composition laws explicitly.

The Terms adapter lowers to LBNF through cesta module-grammar. The native grammar
metadata then exposes categories, projected constructors, ordered argument
sorts, lexical declarations and transparent/list projections. This is the
explicit syntax boundary into the shared sorted GSLT/codec model. Presentation
equations lower to sorted constructor templates at that boundary.

CeTTa's source-driven ParserPack compiler consumes the operational LanguageDef
representation; its current interface does not directly read these .module
files. A downstream adapter must translate the same lowered declarations into
that representation and report its supported fragment. In particular, C's
typedef feedback and scope profile are separate from first-order syntax and
cannot be dropped in that translation. Full native CeTTa ParserPack admission of
Cesta's C profile is not a claimed property of this presentation interface.

Qualification counts compact coverage over original AST constructor
occurrences. Absorbed wrapper constructors count as covered; ordered lists and
lexical tokens are separate. The >=95% coverage and <=1.6 aggregate nonlayout
payload/C-byte gates apply to compact-c/1 and compact-c/2 separately on each
corpus. compact-c/2 is also gated on naturalness: at most 1% of its list heads
on each corpus may be a grammar constructor's name (a hyphenated head equal to
the kebab-case of the constructor label it spells) rather than a C spelling.
Other presentations publish their own measurements.

Ordinary make builds mixed C/.cesta sources through cesta.mk and native compilers.
The emitted program links no Cesta runtime. Dependency files name authored
sources and native headers. Presentation work happens during the build.

Lossless source/1 documents also build through cesta cc. Their decoded main
file supplies C source bytes; the document path supplies its file identity,
quoted-include directory and file-name builtins. Main-file self-inclusion uses
those supplied bytes again. The preprocessor emits .i files, and native target,
optimization and link flags remain in force. Mixed source/1, compact and C
inputs share that route when a source document is present. Plain C builds
without a source document retain the ordinary compiler route.

Generated .i files depend on their complete expanded contents and are published
atomically. Make dependencies name original inputs and actually read headers,
including empty headers; -MMD/-MM omit system headers. Leading ./ is omitted
from dependency spellings. This source/1 build route does not provide compact
directive editing, conditional-alternative admission or macro-use folding.

Generic Lean inverse and switching laws, kernel admission of actual rule/schema
data, independent case replay, corpus tree laws and matching native objects are
separate evidence. These do not assert a universal proof of the native parser,
scope implementation, wire implementation or C compiler semantics.
